screens.title: Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow is the part of your program that decides what happens next, and when something should repeat. On a Raspberry Pi you use it to respond to button presses, read sensors periodically, or run a continuously updating main loop. In this chapter you'll learn how to check conditions with if, elif and else, how to loop over sequences with for and to run an open-ended loop with while, and how to safely stop a running program. We'll use a thermostat-style example so you can see condition checks in a concrete context, and a conveyor-belt analogy to understand repeated actions and loop control. You will also see how to combine these ideas into a main loop that reads inputs, updates outputs, and sleeps to avoid busy-waiting. Finally, we'll cover loop controls like break and continue that handle special cases. By the end you will know the basic patterns that let your Pi move from passive scripts to interactive, long-running programs you can stop and inspect. Ready to explore how decision and repetition shape your projects?

screens.title: What is control flow?
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow describes two complementary abilities: deciding which code runs next, and repeating code when needed. A decision uses conditionals such as if, elif and else to run a block only when a condition holds. Repetition uses loops like for to iterate known sequences and while to repeat until some condition changes. For a Raspberry Pi, decision logic decides whether an LED should turn on or an alert should print, and loops let the Pi check sensors continuously. A common misconception is that loops and conditionals are interchangeable; they are not. A conditional runs once when reached, while a loop repeats multiple times and may be left with break. Another common error is wrong indentation: Python uses indentation to group statements, so an indented line belongs to the branch above it. For a concrete thermostat example, imagine a temperature value of 28. The code checks if temperature is greater than 25 and prints a warm message, otherwise it checks the next condition, and finally uses else for colder cases. Tip: test each branch by feeding different sample values and tracing which print outputs appear. How would you test the cold branch? This question helps you check your understanding.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Control flow = decisions (if/elif/else) + repetition (for/while); indentation matters.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is control flow?
Definition

Control flow in plain terms

Decisions pick which code runs. Loops repeat work. Together they let your Pi react and continue doing tasks until you stop it.

Common misconception
Loops and conditionals serve different goals. A conditional does not repeat; a loop does. Don’t use if when you need repetition.
Why indentation matters
In Python, indentation groups lines into the branch or loop body. Misaligned indentation changes program behavior and often causes errors.
Key Takeaway

Think of conditionals as forks and loops as repeaters — both are essential for interactive Pi programs.

Concrete example
temperature = 28.0
if temperature > 25.0:
    print("It is warm.")
elif temperature > 20.0:
    print("It is comfortable.")
else:
    print("It is cold.")
Run this example with different temperature values to confirm which branch prints. Try 28.0, 22.0, and 18.0 to exercise each branch.
Check your understanding
  • What prints when temperature is 25.0?
  • How would you add a new branch for very warm temperatures above 30?

screens.title: if vs elif vs else
screens.narratorSegment: Chaining conditional checks correctly is essential for predictable behavior. The if statement starts a check, an elif provides an additional exclusive test, and else runs only if none of the earlier conditions was true. Think of them as an ordered checklist where the first matching condition wins. A common mistake is writing overlapping conditions that make later branches unreachable. For example, if you check temperature greater than 20 before checking greater than 25, the greater-than-25 case will never be reached when 28 is tested, if the first condition was broader. Another error is placing else too early, which prevents further checks. Indentation groups the code that runs for each branch; incorrect indentation can attach statements to the wrong branch. As a practical test, change sample temperatures and trace which branch executes to validate your logic. Also remember else has no condition — it catches everything not matched earlier. When you need multiple independent checks, use separate if statements instead of elif. Consider a light and motion sensor: you may need to check both independently, not as ordered alternatives. What situation on your Pi needs independent checks rather than an elif chain?

keyIdea.text: Use if→elif→else as an ordered checklist. For independent checks, use separate if statements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › if vs elif vs else
Comparison

Ordered checks vs independent checks

If you want only one branch to run, chain with elif. If you want multiple checks to run independently, use separate if statements.

Mistake: overlapping conditions
Put specific checks before broader ones to avoid unreachable branches.
When to use separate ifs
Use this when multiple sensors should trigger independent actions, such as logging and alerting both happening together.
Key Takeaway

Order matters in chained checks; use separate checks when events are independent.

Example
temperature = 28
# correct order
if temperature > 30:
    print("Very warm")
elif temperature > 25:
    print("Warm")
elif temperature > 20:
    print("Comfortable")
else:
    print("Cold")

# independent checks
if motion_detected:
    print("Motion logged")
if light_level < low_threshold:
    print("Turn on light")
Test both patterns. Use independent ifs when both actions could happen for the same input set.

screens.title: for loops and range()
screens.narratorSegment: For loops run a block for every item in a sequence. In Python you commonly iterate over lists or use range to generate numeric sequences. Use for when you know the collection you want to walk through, such as a list of sensor names or values. For example, if sensors = ['temperature', 'humidity', 'light'], a for loop prints each reading name once, which is useful for polling or logging. Range is the simplest way to create a numeric sequence to iterate over indexes or to repeat a fixed number of times. A common novice mistake is modifying the list inside the loop in ways that unexpectedly change iteration; avoid removing items while iterating the same list. Another common confusion is expecting for to return a value; it only runs a block per item. For loops are deterministic: the number of iterations equals the number of items in the sequence. Practice by writing a for loop that prints numbers from zero to four using range(5) and then by iterating a short sensor list to simulate readings. What output do you expect from range(3)?

keyIdea.text: Use for to repeat a block for each item in a sequence; use range to generate numeric sequences.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › for loops & range()
Process

Iterating sequences

For loops execute once per item in a sequence. Use lists for named items and range for numeric sequences or fixed repeats.

Practical tip
If you need to modify a list while iterating, iterate over a copy or build a new list to avoid surprising behavior.
Use case
Loop over sensor names to perform the same read-and-log operation without duplicating code.
Key Takeaway

For loops give concise, readable iteration for lists and ranges; choose the right loop for the job.

Examples
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

sensors = ["temperature", "humidity", "light"]
for sensor in sensors:
    print(f"Reading {sensor}...")
First example prints numbers zero through four. Second iterates three sensor names. Try changing the list and re-running to see different outputs.

screens.title: while loops and open-ended repetition
screens.narratorSegment: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. Use while when you don't know ahead of time how many iterations you need, for example when waiting for a sensor to cross a threshold or for a user action to occur. A typical pattern sets a counter or checks a changing value, executes the loop body, then updates the condition so the loop can finish. Forgetting to update the condition leads to an infinite loop. On Raspberry Pi projects, while True creates a main loop that runs until the user stops it. To avoid busy-waiting and high C P U usage, include a small sleep inside the loop when appropriate. The while example here counts from zero to four by incrementing a counter each loop. Practice tracing the loop: list the values the counter takes and when the loop ends. Also note how break can exit a while early and continue skips to the next iteration. Later screens show examples where break stops a loop based on consecutive high sensor readings. What would happen if you forgot the increment step in the counting example? Answering that helps you spot infinite-loop bugs.

keyIdea.text: Use while for open-ended repetition; remember to update the condition or include a stop mechanism.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › while loops
Code Walkthrough

while for open-ended repetition

Use while when the number of repeats depends on runtime state. Update the condition each loop to avoid infinite loops, and include sleep when polling hardware.

Practical warning
Infinite loops are common when the condition never becomes false. Use deliberate updates and test with print statements before deploying on hardware.
When to use while True
Main program loops that should run until the user stops can use while True combined with exception handling for a safe shutdown.
Key Takeaway

While loops are powerful for ongoing tasks, but require explicit updates, pauses, or break conditions to avoid locking the program.

Example
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1
Trace the loop to verify output: zero, one, two, three, four. If you omit the increment you will create an infinite loop and the program will not progress.

screens.title: break and continue
screens.narratorSegment: Loop-control keywords let you handle special cases without complex nesting. Use break to exit a loop immediately when a condition requires stopping, and use continue to skip the remainder of the current iteration and move to the next. In a conveyor-belt analogy, continue is like skipping a damaged item on the belt and moving on to the next one, while break stops the belt because of a fatal error. On the Pi, you might break when a sensor reports a critical failure and you must shut down or switch to a safe state. You might continue when a reading is invalid and you want to ignore it but keep processing further items. A common misuse is relying heavily on breaks and continues in long loops, which can make code harder to read; prefer clear conditions where possible. Practice by iterating a sequence and using continue to skip negative values, and break when a sentinel value appears. This pattern is useful in real sensor processing: skip transient noise but stop for sustained critical readings. What rule will you use to decide between break and continue in your projects?

keyIdea.title: Loop control
keyIdea.text: Use continue to skip an iteration and break to exit early; both help handle exceptional cases cleanly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › break & continue
Process Flow

Skip or stop: handle special cases

Use continue to ignore the rest of the iteration and move on, and break to stop a loop entirely. Both are useful for sensor data validation and emergency stops.

Conveyor-belt analogy
Continue skips one item on the belt; break shuts the belt down because of a problem.
Readability tip
Use clear conditions and limit break/continue usage to keep loops understandable.
Key Takeaway

Break when you must stop the loop now; continue when you want to skip the current item but keep processing.

Examples
values = [3, -1, 5, 99, 2]
for v in values:
    if v < 0:
        continue  # skip invalid reading
    if v == 99:
        print("Critical value, stopping")
        break
    print(v)
In this example negative values are ignored, and a sentinel critical value stops processing entirely. Try changing the list to see how continue and break alter output.

screens.title: Main loop pattern on Raspberry Pi
screens.narratorSegment: Many Raspberry Pi programs use a main loop that runs forever until you stop it. The canonical pattern is while True combined with a sleep to pace work and a try/except around the loop to catch a keyboard interrupt and perform cleanup. This structure keeps your code responsive, reduces C P U usage when polling hardware, and allows you to release resources on exit. A simple main loop reads sensors, updates outputs, and sleeps for a predictable interval. A common beginner mistake is omitting the sleep, which can create a tight loop that overwhelms the C P U or the hardware interface. Another mistake is not handling the keyboard interrupt, which leaves the Pi in an uncertain state when you stop the program. The try/except approach prints a stop message and can gracefully close files or GPIO resources. As practice, write a while True loop that prints Running, sleeps for one second, and handle Ctrl+C to print Stopped. This pattern is the backbone for many small projects and ensures maintainable long-running behavior. Main loop pattern on Raspberry Pi means use while true with sleep and try/except keyboardinterrupt for long-running pi applications and safe shutdown.. In practical terms, a safe, readable program that runs until you stop it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Main loop
keyIdea.text: Use while True with sleep and try/except KeyboardInterrupt for long-running Pi applications and safe shutdown.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Main loop pattern
Architecture

A safe long-running loop

Wrap a while True loop with try/except to catch user stop commands, include sleep to pace work, and keep sensor reads inside the loop for steady updates.

Resource cleanup
On stop, close files and reset GPIO where needed to leave hardware in a safe state.
Sleep to reduce load
A short sleep between iterations avoids high CPU use and gives hardware time to settle between reads.
Key Takeaway

A predictable, interruptible main loop is a reliable foundation for Raspberry Pi applications.

Example
from time import sleep

try:
    while True:
        print("Running...")
        sleep(1)
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    print("Stopped by user.")
Run this on your Pi to see the loop and practice stopping with Ctrl+C. Add sensor reads inside the loop for a continuous monitoring script.

For each value, use an if to print a warning when the reading exceeds thirty degrees. This immediate conditional alerts you to high temperatures. A common expansion is to count how many readings exceed the threshold; increment a counter whenever you see a high value. If you need to stop early when three consecutive readings are too high, track consecutive highs and break the loop when that count reaches three. The important distinctions to practice are resetting the consecutive counter when you encounter a normal reading, and stopping when the consecutive limit is met. A frequent bug is failing to reset the consecutive counter, causing early or late triggers. After you implement this, run the script with simulated input to confirm the loop exits at the expected time and the prints match your reasoning. keyIdea.title: Thermostat pattern
keyIdea.text: Combine loop iteration with conditionals and a consecutive counter to warn and stop early on sustained high readings.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Thermostat example
Activity

Warn above threshold and stop on three consecutive highs

This activity shows how to combine a for loop and conditionals to detect sustained high readings and stop early using a consecutive counter and break.

Common bug
Not resetting consecutive counters causes false triggers. Reset to zero when a reading is below threshold.
Practical tip
Simulate readings first before hooking sensors to avoid hardware surprises and to confirm logic works.
Key Takeaway

Track consecutive events to detect sustained conditions and use break to stop processing early when needed.

Starter code
temps = [29, 31, 32, 33, 28, 31]
consecutive = 0
for t in temps:
    if t > 30:
        print("Warning: high temp", t)
        consecutive += 1
    else:
        consecutive = 0
    if consecutive == 3:
        print("Three consecutive highs: stopping early")
        break
Run this code and observe when the loop breaks. Modify the list to test edge cases where highs are not consecutive.

screens.title: Iterating dictionaries, ranges, and nested loops
screens.narratorSegment: You will often iterate over dictionaries, ranges, and nested sequences. Iterating a dictionary by default yields keys, which is useful for checking or updating mapped sensor thresholds. Use items() to get both key and value when you need both at once. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Iterating collections
Comparison

Lists, dicts, ranges, and nested loops

Choose the iteration style that matches your data: lists for ordered items, dictionaries for key/value maps, and range for numeric sequences. Nested loops handle multiple dimensions like a grid of coordinates.

Dict iteration
Use for k, v in mydict.items() to access both key and value while iterating a dictionary.
Nested loop note
The inner loop completes all iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop. Trace with small ranges to confirm order.
Key Takeaway

Pick the iteration form to match your data, and trace nested loops to predict output order.

Examples
thresholds = {"temp":30, "humidity":70}
for k, v in thresholds.items():
    print(k, "->", v)

for r in range(3):
    for c in range(3):
        print(f"({r},{c})")
The nested loop example prints nine coordinate pairs. Use small ranges when tracing to confirm the printed order.

screens.title: Polling, sleeping, and safe sensor reading
screens.narratorSegment: When your Pi reads sensors in a loop you must balance responsiveness with resource use. Polling too frequently can cause excessive C P U usage or noisy readings; placing a short sleep in the loop gives hardware time to update and reduces load. The example sleep(1) pauses the loop for one second which is often a sensible default for slow-changing sensors. Another practical point is to validate readings and skip invalid samples with continue rather than allowing them to corrupt your logic. When interacting with GPIO or external libraries, ensure your main loop handles exceptions so the program can clean up resources on exit. If you run on real hardware, test with simulated inputs first to verify logic without risking the device. For user-facing loops, provide clear logging so you can trace behavior in the field. Finally, keep loops simple and well-documented so anyone reading your code can understand the decision and timing choices. Which sleep interval will you choose for your sensor based on how fast it changes? Reflecting on that helps you pick a safe polling rate. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Polling & Best Practices
Best Practices

Sleep, validate, and clean up

Use sleep to pace polling, validate sensor values before using them, and handle exceptions to release hardware resources on stop.

Validate inputs
Check for None or out-of-range values and continue to skip them rather than letting invalid data propagate.
Logging
Add simple prints for development so you can trace loop behavior and timing issues in the field.
Key Takeaway

Practical loop hygiene avoids CPU waste, noisy readings, and hardware misconfiguration on stop.

Example
from time import sleep

while True:
    reading = read_sensor()
    if reading is None:
        continue
    process(reading)
    sleep(1)
This pattern validates the reading before processing and sleeps to pace the loop. Replace sleep interval based on sensor characteristics.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep this quick reference handy as you code. First, if, elif and else are ordered checks: the first matching condition runs and else catches everything left. Second, for loops iterate each item in a sequence deterministically, while while loops repeat until a condition changes or until you break. Third, break and continue let you handle special cases inside loops, but use them sparingly to keep code readable. For practical Raspberry Pi work, always include a short sleep in polling loops, validate sensor readings before processing, and wrap main loops in try/except to stop cleanly with a keyboard interrupt. These three rules help you design scripts that respond correctly, run efficiently, and stop safely on real hardware. fullNarratorScript:
Control flow is the part of your program that decides what happens next, and when something should repeat. On a Raspberry Pi you use it to respond to button presses, read sensors periodically, or run a continuously updating main loop. In this chapter you'll learn how to check conditions with if, elif and else, how to loop over sequences with for and to run an open-ended loop with while, and how to safely stop a running program. We'll use a thermostat-style example so you can see condition checks in a concrete context, and a conveyor-belt analogy to understand repeated actions and loop control. You will also see how to combine these ideas into a main loop that reads inputs, updates outputs, and sleeps to avoid busy-waiting. Finally, we'll cover loop controls like break and continue that handle special cases. By the end you will know the basic patterns that let your Pi move from passive scripts to interactive, long-running programs you can stop and inspect. Ready to explore how decision and repetition shape your projects?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write simple decision logic and repeating code for Raspberry Pi projects. First, you will use if, elif and else to check conditions and run different code paths, which matters when your program must react differently to sensor values or button input. Second, you will write for and while loops to repeat actions; for loops iterate sequences like lists and ranges, while loops repeat until a condition changes. Third, you will iterate over lists and dictionaries and know when to use range for numeric sequences, which helps when processing multiple sensors or data items. Fourth, you will apply control flow to practical Raspberry Pi tasks such as threshold logic for a thermostat or menu navigation and understand how to stop a main loop safely. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can confirm you can both write and reason about the code in real projects.

This roadmap gives a short practice plan for each objective so you can verify you know how to use control flow in real Pi tasks. For conditionals, write a thermostat script that reads a temperature value and prints warm, comfortable, or cold. Run it with several sample values to see each branch execute, and check your indentation. For loops, write a for loop over a list of sensor names and print each reading name; then write a while loop that counts until a limit. For data iteration, use range to print numeric sequences and iterate a small dictionary of sensor thresholds to produce alerts. For applied skills, combine a loop with a conditional so the program reads a list of temperature values, warns when above 30 degrees, counts consecutive high readings, and stops early if three arrive in a row. Each practice gives a clear expected output you can trace or run on your Raspberry Pi to confirm competency.

Control flow describes two complementary abilities: deciding which code runs next, and repeating code when needed. A decision uses conditionals such as if, elif and else to run a block only when a condition holds. Repetition uses loops like for to iterate known sequences and while to repeat until some condition changes. For a Raspberry Pi, decision logic decides whether an LED should turn on or an alert should print, and loops let the Pi check sensors continuously. A common misconception is that loops and conditionals are interchangeable; they are not. A conditional runs once when reached, while a loop repeats multiple times and may be left with break. Another common error is wrong indentation: Python uses indentation to group statements, so an indented line belongs to the branch above it. For a concrete thermostat example, imagine a temperature value of 28. The code checks if temperature is greater than 25 and prints a warm message, otherwise it checks the next condition, and finally uses else for colder cases. Tip: test each branch by feeding different sample values and tracing which print outputs appear. How would you test the cold branch? This question helps you check your understanding.

Chaining conditional checks correctly is essential for predictable behavior. The if statement starts a check, an elif provides an additional exclusive test, and else runs only if none of the earlier conditions was true. Think of them as an ordered checklist where the first matching condition wins. A common mistake is writing overlapping conditions that make later branches unreachable. For example, if you check temperature greater than 20 before checking greater than 25, the greater-than-25 case will never be reached when 28 is tested, if the first condition was broader. Another error is placing else too early, which prevents further checks. Indentation groups the code that runs for each branch; incorrect indentation can attach statements to the wrong branch. As a practical test, change sample temperatures and trace which branch executes to validate your logic. Also remember else has no condition — it catches everything not matched earlier. When you need multiple independent checks, use separate if statements instead of elif. Consider a light and motion sensor: you may need to check both independently, not as ordered alternatives. What situation on your Pi needs independent checks rather than an elif chain?

For loops run a block for every item in a sequence. In Python you commonly iterate over lists or use range to generate numeric sequences. Use for when you know the collection you want to walk through, such as a list of sensor names or values. For example, if sensors = ['temperature', 'humidity', 'light'], a for loop prints each reading name once, which is useful for polling or logging. Range is the simplest way to create a numeric sequence to iterate over indexes or to repeat a fixed number of times. A common novice mistake is modifying the list inside the loop in ways that unexpectedly change iteration; avoid removing items while iterating the same list. Another common confusion is expecting for to return a value; it only runs a block per item. For loops are deterministic: the number of iterations equals the number of items in the sequence. Practice by writing a for loop that prints numbers from zero to four using range(5) and then by iterating a short sensor list to simulate readings. What output do you expect from range(3)?

A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. Use while when you don't know ahead of time how many iterations you need, for example when waiting for a sensor to cross a threshold or for a user action to occur. A typical pattern sets a counter or checks a changing value, executes the loop body, then updates the condition so the loop can finish. Forgetting to update the condition leads to an infinite loop. On Raspberry Pi projects, while True creates a main loop that runs until the user stops it. To avoid busy-waiting and high C P U usage, include a small sleep inside the loop when appropriate. The while example here counts from zero to four by incrementing a counter each loop. Practice tracing the loop: list the values the counter takes and when the loop ends. Also note how break can exit a while early and continue skips to the next iteration. Later screens show examples where break stops a loop based on consecutive high sensor readings. What would happen if you forgot the increment step in the counting example? Answering that helps you spot infinite-loop bugs.

Loop-control keywords let you handle special cases without complex nesting. Use break to exit a loop immediately when a condition requires stopping, and use continue to skip the remainder of the current iteration and move to the next. In a conveyor-belt analogy, continue is like skipping a damaged item on the belt and moving on to the next one, while break stops the belt because of a fatal error. On the Pi, you might break when a sensor reports a critical failure and you must shut down or switch to a safe state. You might continue when a reading is invalid and you want to ignore it but keep processing further items. A common misuse is relying heavily on breaks and continues in long loops, which can make code harder to read; prefer clear conditions where possible. Practice by iterating a sequence and using continue to skip negative values, and break when a sentinel value appears. This pattern is useful in real sensor processing: skip transient noise but stop for sustained critical readings. What rule will you use to decide between break and continue in your projects?

Many Raspberry Pi programs use a main loop that runs forever until you stop it. The canonical pattern is while True combined with a sleep to pace work and a try/except around the loop to catch a keyboard interrupt and perform cleanup. This structure keeps your code responsive, reduces C P U usage when polling hardware, and allows you to release resources on exit. A simple main loop reads sensors, updates outputs, and sleeps for a predictable interval. A common beginner mistake is omitting the sleep, which can create a tight loop that overwhelms the C P U or the hardware interface. Another mistake is not handling the keyboard interrupt, which leaves the Pi in an uncertain state when you stop the program. The try/except approach prints a stop message and can gracefully close files or GPIO resources. As practice, write a while True loop that prints Running, sleeps for one second, and handle Ctrl+C to print Stopped. This pattern is the backbone for many small projects and ensures maintainable long-running behavior. Main loop pattern on Raspberry Pi means use while true with sleep and try/except keyboardinterrupt for long-running pi applications and safe shutdown.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
